name: Panegyric-Ruin

civilization.name: The Laudation
civilization.notes: A civilization that built monumental architecture celebrating their own achievements. Their monuments survive on a world that their industrial activity rendered barren. They appear to have known what they were doing and did it anyway.

geological_features: Artificial mountain formations from mining tailings
specific_features: Monumental architecture celebrating an extinct civilization's achievements
Self-inflicted environmental devastation visible from orbit
description: Panegyric-Ruin is a barren world that was made barren, not born that way. The geological record shows a planet that was once temperate and habitable, its transformation into wasteland the work of its own inhabitants. The Laudation strip-mined their continental shelves so thoroughly that the topography is visibly artificial from orbit, replacing natural landscapes with terraced extraction pits and mountains of mining tailings. Depleted aquifer systems underlie the surface, their water consumed by industrial processes that left contaminated residue in its place.

Rising above the devastation, the Laudation's monuments endure. Massive sculptural complexes celebrate their civilization's achievements in materials engineered to outlast the planet's geology: towers commemorating engineering milestones, plazas inscribed with production records, and a colossus near the equator whose outstretched arms span three kilometers, its face turned to the sky with an expression that might be triumph or defiance. They built their monuments to last and succeeded beyond any reasonable expectation.

The archaeological record tells a story of a civilization that understood what it was doing. Late-period inscriptions explicitly acknowledge the environmental cost of their industrial expansion and celebrate it as the price of progress. The Laudation appears to have made a deliberate choice: they would consume their world in exchange for achievement, and they would build monuments to ensure that achievement was remembered after the world could no longer sustain them. They did not survive, but their monuments did.

Panegyric-Ruin serves as a philosophical touchstone for debates about sustainability and legacy. The Laudation's technology was sophisticated enough that they could have chosen a different path, and their records make clear they knew this. The monuments are studied not just as archaeological artifacts but as arguments, each one a statement about what a civilization owes to the future versus what it claims for the present. The planet has no remaining resources worth extracting; the Laudation saw to that. All it has left are the monuments and the questions they pose.
